The Alberses buy pre-Columbian pieces from local people near the pyramids: people show up with handkerchiefs full of objects. Many sites were not yet known.
Louis Adamic's visit to the college

A Yugoslav-born journalist, a Guggenheim fellow for three years, Adamic flees the “tempo and confusion” of New York on a pastoral road trip through the South; a friend at the Guggenheim Foundation steers him toward BMC. He is given a guest room and an invitation to dinner; the table conversation goes on well past midnight. A visit of a few days stretches into two and a half months.

The Alberses' first trip to Mexico

The Alberses visit Mexico for the first time; they will return often throughout their lives and develop an immense respect for the arts and architecture of ancient cultures, notably archaeological sites such as Monte Alban.
Two years after their arrival, the Alberses feel truly at home in the New World for the first time; Mexico has kept its Indian heritage and stands apart from Europe.
First trip to Mexico and first purchase

During the summer vacation, in the Dreiers' secondhand Ford Model A convertible, they take the only road available: Laredo, then due south to Mexico City and Oaxaca. One day, while Anni waits in the car as the other three visit a church, a little boy offers to sell her a kid goat or a small figurine head wrapped in a handkerchief; she buys the head for a few pesos.

A student and collaborator of Oskar Schlemmer at the Bauhaus, Schawinsky stages several original productions of nonnarrative, participatory theater at the college, including Spectodrama in 1936, then Danse Macabre: A Sociological Study in 1938.

A few months after his arrival, Schawinsky organizes a nonnarrative theater of “total experience”: storyboarded skits rehearsed through improvisation, each assigned to a category (optics, form and color, acoustics, sound, language, music, time, space, architecture, technology, illusion), with music by Schwitters (Ursonate, 1922-32).

Publication of Adamic's article in Harper's
The article appears in Harper's with a scathing, sardonic reply by Bernard DeVoto attacking Black Mountain and earlier intentional communities; it is later condensed in Reader's Digest.

After two and a half months in the community, Adamic writes that Black Mountain is hard to describe: it must be lived; he reports Rice's phrase on method versus content and Albers's on bringing out the artist in everyone.

Purchase of the Lake Eden estate

The college buys a property three miles from the Blue Ridge Assembly, around the artificial Lake Eden: acres of farmland and woodland bordering the lake, dotted with rustic cottages, with a large building that includes a dining hall. The college ceases to be a tenant and dreams of a permanent, year-round existence.

The college buys a vast estate on the shore of Lake Eden (also presented as the former Lake Eden Inn); it lacks insulation and individual studies, forcing it to operate as a “mobile campus” for four years.
Purchase of the Lake Eden land
north of the village of Black Mountain

The college buys its own property as insurance against the possible cancellation of the lease on the Blue Ridge site. Lake Eden had been a camp and summer resort; rustic buildings: two lodges, a dining hall overlooking the lake, several cottages.
Lake Eden, the valley across from Blue Ridge

First step toward a permanent home: purchase of the Lake Eden property, a former summer resort a few kilometers across the valley from Blue Ridge. The money is raised through a special appeal to sympathizers, the Forbes family being particularly generous.

Meeting Elaine Fried

De Kooning meets Elaine Fried, a nineteen-year-old art student. Burckhardt: “I think it was love at first sight. Soon they were living together, painting together, holding off the landlord, getting married, and were as close as two people can be.” Elaine and her sister Marjorie sometimes pose for his drawings and paintings.
